pages.text: $(l)The recommended way:$() a Storage Bus on an Export Interface. It outperforms partitioned interfaces and subnet proxies, and up to 5 networks can storage-bus the same Export Interface without linking.

$(li)Don't use dual interfaces with storage buses to link subnets; they double-count and are unstable.$(li)Always filter the Storage Bus to what the subnet should see; unfiltered connections risk item loops, lag and wrong behavior.
$(li)A controller on the subnet isn't strictly required, but you usually want one.

$(l)Keep subnets small and purpose-built$()$(li)Only include items needed for one task (e.g., alloy smelting or seed crafting).$(li)Large subnets force frequent recipe tree recomputations, causing lag.$(li)For crafting on a subnet, use Export Interfaces with push cards to feed assemblers/injectors.

$(l)Import and Export Interfaces$()$(li)Import Interfaces have small capacity—use multiple around high-output sources (e.g., EnderIO miners) to scale throughput.$(li)Import and export interfaces do $(o)not$() support priority settings—they act as masters, not AE2 priority participants.
$(li)Interfaces respect NBT (including damage): partially damaged items won’t stack and may jam the system; don’t rely on them to repair or combine items.

$(li)Shift-clicking into an import interface during polling cycles may temporarily show stacks >64 in your inventory—harmless but visually odd.$(li)Do not click on universal interfaces—they can cause crashes.

$(l)Other tips$()$(li)The best way to reach EMC is a Storage Bus directly on an EMC Link.$(li)Ensure all network components are chunkloaded; missing chunks cause erratic behavior.$(li)One wireless connector output can feed several wireless connector inputs.
